title: Pointer Safety and Ownership
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and core rule of pointer safety and ownership using at least one example.
Trace or adapt a minimal C++ example related to pointer safety and ownership and state its expected result.
Identify one precondition, error case, lifetime issue, portability assumption or version constraint relevant to the topic.

content.intro: Pointer Safety and Ownership focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.
content.why_it_matters: Pointer Safety and Ownership matters because before dereferencing or storing an alias, identify the owner, the lifetime and the conditions under which access remains valid. Connect this lesson to the earlier module prerequisites and use it as a building block rather than an isolated term.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
Pointers and references provide indirect access, but the object’s lifetime and ownership remain central. Prefer value semantics and standard ownership types before manual allocation.

Pointer Safety and Ownership focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.

Before dereferencing or storing an alias, identify the owner, the lifetime and the conditions under which access remains valid.

content_blocks.title: Minimal example: Pointer Safety and Ownership
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as `example.cpp`. Compile using `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic example.cpp -o example; then run ./example (Windows: .\example.exe).` The CodeLeaf page shows reference output only; it does not execute C++ learner code.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the example, rebuild with the same standard and warning flags, and rerun the same input. If the example is nondeterministic or depends on platform support, record that constraint instead of expecting byte-for-byte identical output.
content_blocks.limitations: The built-in CodeLeaf page does not execute C++ in a sandbox. Compile local teaching examples only; arbitrary learner code requires a separately deployed isolated runner with CPU, memory, process, filesystem and network limits.
content_blocks.explanation: unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership and releases the object automatically when the owner leaves scope.

items.title: Owning and Non-Owning Pointers
items.text: A pointer can refer to an object or function, or hold a null value; dereference only a valid pointer while the referred object is alive.

content_blocks.title: Guided practice
content_blocks.text: Before changing the example, predict the output and name the rule that produces it. Then modify one line to demonstrate owning and non-owning pointers, and add a test for one boundary or failure scenario. Keep the experiment small enough that another learner can reproduce it.

content_blocks.title: Version, safety and portability note
content_blocks.text: Use standard C++ rather than compiler-specific behavior unless the lesson explicitly labels the dependency. Feature support varies by compiler version and standard-library implementation. Check the references and prefer explicit diagnostics to assumptions.

content.task: Create a small, independent example that demonstrates pointer safety and ownership. Predict the result before compiling, write down a precondition, and test one ordinary case plus one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example builds under a documented standard mode with warnings enabled.
The predicted and observed result are recorded; deviations are explained.
At least one boundary, invalid-input, lifetime or portability assumption is tested or documented.
hints: Start with the smallest example that demonstrates owning and non-owning pointers.
Trace the relevant values and state the expected output before running the program.
Check the standard/compiler reference and add an edge case instead of relying only on the happy path.
summary: Pointer Safety and Ownership is about a concrete language rule or engineering decision, not only terminology.
Keep the important preconditions and trade-offs visible when applying pointer safety and ownership.
Use explicit build settings and focused tests to support the claim that the example behaves as expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one successful example proves every case.
common_mistakes.why: It may miss an invalid input, boundary, error path or implementation difference.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the preconditions and test at least one ordinary case plus an edge or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a language feature without checking its requirements.
common_mistakes.why: The code may depend on a standard version, an object lifetime or an API precondition.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the explicit standard mode and verify the relevant rule and compiler/library support.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring compiler diagnostics or simplifying away ownership and error behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Warnings and explicit contracts often expose a defect before it becomes a runtime problem.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with warnings, keep the smallest reproducible sample and state what happens when an operation fails.
